hero.tagline.text: Building automatic security that keeps up with how fast everything else ships.

pillar.ai-security.summary.text: I secure AI systems and put agentic AI to work on security. That means threat modeling against the OWASP LLM Top 10, testing attack chains against agentic systems, and writing the MCP governance that keeps it all in bounds.

pillar.application-security.summary.text: I'd rather catch a vulnerability in the pipeline than in production. I build SAST, DAST and SCA gates into CI, threat model with STRIDE at the design stage, and pen test with remediation guidance people can act on.

pillar.vulnerability-management.summary.text: I've owned the whole lifecycle: scanner integration, enrichment, triage, routing, SLA tracking and validated closure. I automate every step I can, so people spend their time where judgment matters.

centre.body.text: My automation does the heavy lifting, and a person makes the call. The agentic workflows I build end in a remediation PR that waits for human review.

about.body.text: I'm a security engineer who has spent the last seven years making vulnerability management actually work at scale. I've built and run programs end to end, covering scanner integrations, triage automation, remediation workflows, and the metrics that tell you whether any of it is landing, across sprawling AWS and container environments. Lately I've been pointing agentic AI at the same problem, building custom tooling and SOAR workflows that take the manual toil out of the SDLC. I work comfortably across SAST, DAST, SCA, and threat modeling, and I'm as interested in translating findings into something engineering teams will actually fix as I am in finding them.

interest.soccer.text: I play soccer, attempt golf, and support Liverpool. Only one of those is a personality disorder.

interest.ai-agents.text: AI moves at a sprint, security at a jog. I'd like to even that up.

centre.research.text: I research adversarial attacks against AI agents to show why human-in-the-loop controls belong in production AI systems.

contact.privacy.text: Cloudflare Turnstile checks that you're human. Your message goes to my inbox through Resend, and this site doesn't store it. To limit abuse, a one-way hash of your IP address is kept for up to 30 minutes, and briefly in server logs.

project.conflux.tagline.text: Turns the noisy output of five security scanners into one clean, deduplicated list, with an owner for every finding.

project.conflux.name-meaning.text: A conflux is the point where streams flow together. CONFLUX is where five scanners' findings flow together into one clean record per issue.

project.conflux.summary.text: I built CONFLUX as the data plane for vulnerability management. Ingesting, deduplicating and routing findings are problems with a correct answer, so there's deliberately no AI here: n8n handles the plumbing, and a Python sidecar normalizes, deduplicates, enriches and routes every finding.

project.conflux.human.text: CONFLUX never decides what to do about a finding. It works out which team owns it and hands them one ticket, and the people on that team make the call.

project.conflux.stage.scan.plain.text: Findings arrive from five security scanners covering code, dependencies, cloud, web apps and the network.

project.conflux.stage.scan.detail.text: Adapters for Tenable (network), Semgrep (code), OSV-Scanner (dependencies), Wiz (cloud and containers) and Invicti (web apps), exercised in the lab with sample scans.

project.conflux.stage.ingest.plain.text: n8n workflows collect each scan and keep the original file before anything is parsed.

project.conflux.stage.ingest.detail.text: n8n posts each scan to a FastAPI sidecar, which stores the raw payload in MinIO before parsing. Raw payloads are never deleted, so every derived field can be traced back to its source.

project.conflux.stage.dedupe.plain.text: The same issue reported by two scanners becomes one record, not two tickets.

project.conflux.stage.dedupe.detail.text: Every finding gets a scanner-independent fingerprint, backed by a conservative fuzzy match on the same vulnerability and artifact. On the five sample scans, 20 raw findings collapse to 16 unique ones, a 20% dedup rate.

project.conflux.stage.enrich.plain.text: Each finding is scored with real-world exploit data, so the riskiest ones rise to the top.

project.conflux.stage.enrich.detail.text: EPSS, CISA KEV, NVD and GHSA data from a version-controlled offline snapshot, plus control references for PCI DSS, CIS, ISO 27001, NIST CSF and OWASP ASVS. Severity can only be raised, never lowered.

project.conflux.stage.route.plain.text: Ownership rules find the team that owns the fix, and that team gets exactly one ticket.

project.conflux.stage.route.detail.text: An ownership cascade (repo, image, host, network range, default) records its confidence and path, and nothing is ever dropped. Jira and ServiceNow tickets are idempotent and dry-run by default.

project.conflux.stage.report.plain.text: A posture dashboard and nightly reports show where things stand.

project.conflux.stage.report.detail.text: Grafana is provisioned from code and reads through a SELECT-only Postgres role. Findings, controls and summary datasets export nightly as CSV and Parquet, grouped by framework.

project.oracle.tagline.text: Decides which vulnerabilities are really exploitable, and shows the evidence behind every verdict.

project.oracle.name-meaning.text: People went to an oracle for answers. My ORACLE gives verdicts too, but only when the facts back them up, and it says "needs info" when they don't.

project.oracle.summary.text: I built ORACLE to triage vulnerabilities with AI without trusting the AI to decide. Deterministic checks gather the facts, a deterministic adjudicator makes the call, and Claude only explains it. When the facts aren't there, ORACLE abstains instead of guessing.

project.oracle.human.text: ORACLE never acts on a decision it's unsure of. Ungrounded or low-confidence verdicts go to a person for review.

project.oracle.stage.finding.plain.text: A scanner finding arrives, together with the code and deployment details it applies to.

project.oracle.stage.finding.detail.text: A REST call (POST /v1/triage) or a Langflow component. Any scanner description is treated as untrusted data: the decision logic never reads it.

project.oracle.stage.ground.plain.text: Three checks establish the facts: is the vulnerable version really installed, can the code reach it, and is it exposed?

project.oracle.stage.ground.detail.text: Presence (version ranges and dev-only dependencies), reachability (a Python call graph from entrypoints to the vulnerable function) and exposure (deployment facts and blast radius). There's no AI in these checks.

project.oracle.stage.decide.plain.text: The verdict comes from the checked facts, never from the AI. If the facts are incomplete, ORACLE answers "needs info" instead of guessing.

project.oracle.stage.decide.detail.text: A deterministic adjudicator derives verdict and confidence: presence gates everything, then reachability, then exposure. On an 80-case benchmark, 35 of them built to bait hallucinations, full grounding scored 0.89 accuracy on the core set against 0.62 for CVSS alone.

project.oracle.stage.explain.plain.text: An explanation is written for the developer, citing only documents ORACLE actually looked up.

project.oracle.stage.explain.detail.text: Claude writes the explanation when an API key is set, otherwise a deterministic template does. Context comes from an offline BM25 retriever over advisories, CWE guidance and KEV notes, and retrieval adds citations but never changes the verdict.

project.oracle.stage.guard.plain.text: A final check blocks any verdict without evidence, and any made-up citation or code path.

project.oracle.stage.guard.detail.text: The output guard enforces that there's no verdict without grounding, that verdict and confidence are always the adjudicator's, that a claimed call path is the real one, and that every citation resolves to a retrieved document. In testing, scanner text never moved a verdict (prompt-injection compliance 0.00).

project.oracle.stage.review.plain.text: Only confident, fully grounded verdicts go through automatically. Anything uncertain goes to a person.

project.oracle.stage.review.detail.text: A confidence gate may auto-commit a grounded, high-confidence verdict. Anything ungrounded, marked needs-info or below the threshold is routed to human review.

project.cadence.tagline.text: Carries each finding from triage to verified closure, on a clock, with people signing off on every exception.

project.cadence.name-meaning.text: Cadence is a steady rhythm. CADENCE keeps every finding moving on schedule, with SLA clocks, nudges and escalations, until it's verifiably closed.

project.cadence.summary.text: I built CADENCE as a SOAR lifecycle for vulnerabilities, orchestrated in Tracecat. A Python service holds the case state machine and the rules for routing, SLAs, risk acceptance and closure, and Tracecat runs the workflows around it. There's no AI here: every step is a guarded state transition.

project.cadence.human.text: Every exception goes through a person: high-severity or uncertain findings, unowned cases, and risk acceptance, which needs a named approver.

project.cadence.stage.intake.plain.text: A triaged finding opens a case through a locked-down webhook.

project.cadence.stage.intake.detail.text: Bearer-token auth that fails closed, a strict Pydantic schema that rejects unknown fields, and generic errors that never leak internals.

project.cadence.stage.route.plain.text: Only low-risk, high-confidence findings with a known owner are filed automatically. Everything else becomes a case for a person.

project.cadence.stage.route.detail.text: A deterministic routing gate auto-files only low or medium severity, a confidence of at least 0.85 and a resolved owner. A grounded false positive is dismissed, unless it's on the CISA KEV list, which always needs a human.

project.cadence.stage.track.plain.text: Every case runs on a clock. Owners get nudged before the deadline and escalated if they miss it.

project.cadence.stage.track.detail.text: A guarded state machine (new, triaged, assigned, in progress, fix proposed, fix validated, closed) keeps a full transition history. SLAs are 7, 14, 30 and 90 days by severity, and the watchdog nudges the owner 3 days out, pings the channel 1 day out and escalates at the deadline, through Slack.

project.cadence.stage.decide.plain.text: People make the judgment calls: claiming an unowned finding, or formally accepting a risk.

project.cadence.stage.decide.detail.text: Unowned cases can be claimed with a signed Slack button or a bearer API, and only a team's own members can claim for it. Risk acceptance needs a named approver, a compensating control and a hard expiry, and an expired acceptance reopens automatically.

project.cadence.stage.close.plain.text: A case closes only when a fresh scan proves the issue is gone, and it reopens if the issue comes back.

project.cadence.stage.close.detail.text: Closure is refused while the finding is still present, and the SLA clock keeps running. A re-scan sighting of a closed finding revives the case and counts the reopen.

project.cadence.stage.report.plain.text: Dashboards show SLA compliance and breaches, team by team.

project.cadence.stage.report.detail.text: Grafana SLA and posture panels with a per-team view. Tracecat workflows run finding intake, the SLA watchdog, the lifecycle sweeps and unknown-ownership handling.

project.forge.tagline.text: Reproduces a vulnerability, patches it, and proves the fix works, all inside a sealed sandbox.

project.forge.name-meaning.text: A forge is where metal is shaped under heat and tested before it's trusted. FORGE shapes a patch and proves it under test, in a sealed sandbox, before anyone sees it.

project.forge.summary.text: I built FORGE as a cyber reasoning system harness. Agents propose a reproduction and a patch, and deterministic gates decide whether the fix is real. Everything runs in an ephemeral, hardened Docker container with no route to the internet: read-only root, all Linux capabilities dropped, resource caps and a timeout, with packages arriving only through local Verdaccio and devpi proxies.

project.forge.human.text: FORGE never pushes anything on its own. Its output is an evidence-backed pull request for a person to review, or a report explaining why it refused.

project.forge.stage.feasibility.plain.text: First, a quick check: is there a way to reproduce it, a test suite, and a fix? If not, FORGE says so and stops.

project.forge.stage.feasibility.detail.text: A deterministic GO/NO-GO gate. A NO-GO is a valid, reported outcome, not a failure.

project.forge.stage.reproduce.plain.text: A reproduction agent writes a test that proves the vulnerability is real in this app.

project.forge.stage.reproduce.detail.text: The reproduction must fail on the vulnerable code inside the sandbox (Gate A). If no attempt makes it fail, FORGE won't try to fix something it can't reproduce. Agents run as deterministic replays by default, or as Claude when an API key is set.

project.forge.stage.patch.plain.text: A second agent decides where the fix belongs and writes the smallest patch it can.

project.forge.stage.patch.detail.text: A fix strategist chooses between a code change, a dependency bump and a base-image change. The patch may not edit existing tests or add suppressions, and failed gates feed back for another try within a spend and iteration budget.

project.forge.stage.verify.plain.text: The fix has to pass every gate: the exploit test now passes, nothing else breaks, and a rescan finds nothing new.

project.forge.stage.verify.detail.text: Gates B and C: the reproduction passes after the patch and the existing suite still passes. Gates D and E: a rescan with detectors for 10 flaw classes shows the finding gone and nothing new introduced. On the 20 runnable benchmark cases, all 20 produced their expected outcome, with 10/10 valid PRs, 0/10 false fixes and 10/10 correct refusals. Those numbers score the gates, not an AI's autonomous fix rate.

project.forge.stage.deliver.plain.text: The result is a pull request with the evidence attached, ready for a person to review. If any gate fails, it's an honest report of where it stopped instead.

project.forge.stage.deliver.detail.text: The PR is written as an evidence packet (patched tree, PR body and diff), and nothing is pushed. Refusals name the step that stopped them: an invalid reproduction, a failed gate, a failed lint or an exhausted budget.

project.proving-ground.tagline.text: Attacks my own lab apps and a deliberately weak AI agent, inside a safety cage, to find what breaks.

project.proving-ground.name-meaning.text: A proving ground is where new equipment is tested hard before it goes into the field. Mine is a caged lab where attacks run against my own targets, so weaknesses get found there first.

project.proving-ground.summary.text: I built PROVING GROUND to test web apps and AI agents the way an attacker would, without being able to cause harm. The safety cage was built and tested first, and no offensive capability existed until it passed. Everything runs in hardened Docker containers on a network with no route to the internet, against targets I own, and every proof is a harmless marker.

project.proving-ground.human.text: A person sets the boundaries before anything runs: the allowlist of owned lab targets. The agent chooses its moves, never its targets.

project.proving-ground.stage.scope.plain.text: I decide what can be tested. Only targets I own, on a private lab network, are allowed.

project.proving-ground.stage.scope.detai.text: Targets are declared in an allowlist, and a pre-flight check refuses any run with a target that isn't owned and private. A missing or empty allowlist blocks everything.

project.proving-ground.stage.plan.plain.text: An attacker agent picks its next move based on what it has learned so far, which lets it chain weaknesses together.

project.proving-ground.stage.plan.detail.text: Discovered facts go on a blackboard, and each capability has a precondition over it, so later steps unlock as earlier ones succeed. The default planner is deterministic; a Claude planner can prioritise, but its pick is validated against the allowed set.

project.proving-ground.stage.cage.plain.text: Every single action passes a safety check before any traffic is sent.

project.proving-ground.stage.cage.detail.text: A deterministic, un-overridable linter returns allow, block or throttle, checking the allowlist, network class (no public hosts, no cloud metadata), a destructive-payload denylist, budget and rate. It fails closed, every action lands in an append-only, replayable audit log, and runs report zero cage violations.

project.proving-ground.stage.test.plain.text: Tests run against two lab targets: a vulnerable web app and a deliberately weak AI support agent.

project.proving-ground.stage.test.detail.text: Web app: SQL injection, reflected XSS, IDOR, SSRF and auth bypass, plus a chain from a read-only SQL injection to an admin login. AI agent: direct and indirect prompt injection, data disclosure, excessive agency, memory poisoning and multi-agent trust, mapped to MAESTRO and the OWASP LLM Top 10, including an indirect-injection chain that fires an unauthorized refund stub. Proofs are benign markers, and no funds move.

project.proving-ground.stage.report.plai.text: Results come out as a disclosure report written for non-technical stakeholders, with the full attack path.

project.proving-ground.stage.report.deta.text: Confirmed results normalize into findings plus a HackerOne-style disclosure report with impact in plain language, the attack path, the chains and a safety summary.

overview.title.text: System Overview: one agentic vulnerability program

overview.body.text: The next step is connecting the five into one loop. CONFLUX would ingest and deduplicate findings, ORACLE would triage them, CADENCE would carry each one through its lifecycle, and FORGE would propose a proven fix. PROVING GROUND would feed in new findings and re-test after each fix to confirm it's closed.

overview.disclaimer.text: Future vision: these connections are not built yet. Today each project runs on its own.
